query: what is the difference between linear and nonlinear gyrokinetics in terms of simulating growth rates and heat fluxes

rubrics.title: Explain how growth rates are obtained in linear runs
rubrics.description: State that linear simulations are used to extract instability growth rates and frequencies from the early exponential phase, and that these rates are mode-resolved rather than transport-level outputs.

rubrics.title: Explain what nonlinear runs add beyond growth rates
rubrics.description: Describe that nonlinear simulations use the linear instabilities as input but then evolve the cascade, saturation, and self-consistent fluctuation spectrum that determine turbulent transport.

rubrics.title: Distinguish growth-rate prediction from heat-flux prediction
rubrics.description: Make clear that linear results can indicate whether turbulence is likely to exist, but heat flux is a nonlinear transport quantity that generally cannot be predicted quantitatively from linear growth rates alone.

rubrics.title: Relate linear stability to nonlinear heat-flux trends
rubrics.description: Explain the practical link that similar linear growth rates can still correspond to different nonlinear heat fluxes because saturation depends on mode competition, profiles, geometry, and nonlinear interactions.

rubrics.title: Cover comparative validation evidence
rubrics.description: Use the cited studies to note that linear codes are often compared by matching growth rates and frequencies, whereas nonlinear codes are validated by agreement with measured or benchmarked heat fluxes.

rubrics.title: Address role of geometry and profile parameters
rubrics.description: Mention that magnetic geometry, gradients, beta, and related parameters can preserve similar linear growth rates while changing nonlinear heat-flux outcomes, so linear agreement does not guarantee nonlinear agreement.

rubrics.title: State limitations of linear gyrokinetics for transport
rubrics.description: Explicitly note that linear simulations miss saturation mechanisms, zonal-flow regulation, cross-scale coupling, and other nonlinear effects that are essential for predicting heat flux.

rubrics.title: Provide practical guidance on when each approach is used
rubrics.description: Explain that linear gyrokinetics is typically used for fast stability screening and mode identification, while nonlinear gyrokinetics is used when the goal is quantitative prediction of turbulent heat transport.

query: The question concerns the definition of the magnetic field created by a current distributed with uniform density over the cross-section of a semi-cylindrical conductor. rubrics.title: Field contribution of the actual semi-cylindrical conductor
rubrics.description: Compute the magnetic field produced by the current carried in the conducting semicircle itself, not just the idealized full-cylinder case.

rubrics.title: Treatment of material permeability
rubrics.description: Use the correct constitutive relation for a non-magnetic conductor in air and clarify how the busbar’s permeability affects or does not affect the final field at the observation point.

rubrics.title: Direction of the magnetic field

rubrics.title: Closed-form expression at the specified point
rubrics.description: Provide an explicit formula for the magnetic flux density at the upper-left boundary point in terms of I, R, μ0, and any permeability factors if relevant.

rubrics.description: Distinguish whether the evaluation point lies inside the conducting region, on its boundary, or outside it, since the field expression changes with radial location.

rubrics.description: State the idealizations required for the result, such as infinitely long busbar, negligible end effects, quasi-static conditions, and uniform cross-section current distribution.

rubrics.title: Practical computational method
rubrics.description: If an exact Ampère-law shortcut is not available for the semi-cylindrical shape, describe a workable method such as decomposing into simpler current distributions or integrating Biot–Savart over the semicircular cross-section.

query: Soft-biometric privacy-enhancement methods are commonly used in face recognition systems to prevent attackers from inferring users’ soft-biometric attributes (e.g., gender, age, and race). However, existing methods are often limited to protecting privacy at either the representation or image level. We propose a novel Face Conditional Privacy Funnel Network (Face-CPFNet), a multi-level privacy-enhancement framework that disentangles a sensitive attribute from face representations and reconstructs privacy-enhanced images. Face-CPFNet introduces three key innovations: First, it considers a privacy protection system in which attackers receive representation data designed to conceal the sensitive attribute of users. The reconstructed images are generated based on the attacker’s guess of the potential label value of the sensitive attribute. Second, it leverages the conditional privacy funnel principle with mutual information to optimize the privacy channel, parameterized by deep neural networks using a variational approximation approach. For a discrete binary sensitive attribute, the privacy channel aims to minimize the Jensen-Shannon divergence of the probability distributions associated with the latent representations for each label. Finally, it enables supervised disentangled representation learning for a sensitive attribute to generate semantically meaningful images from these representations. Experimental results on benchmark face datasets demonstrate that Face-CPFNet effectively balances face verification accuracy with soft-biometric privacy. summary

rubrics.title: Problem framing and threat model
rubrics.description: A strong answer must clearly explain the privacy-enhancement setting Face-CPFNet targets, including that attackers receive protected representations and may also infer the sensitive attribute label used for image reconstruction.

rubrics.description: A strong answer must describe how the method protects privacy at both the representation level and the reconstructed-image level, and why this goes beyond methods limited to only one layer.

rubrics.description: A strong answer must explain the conditional privacy funnel principle used to optimize the privacy channel, including the role of mutual information in suppressing sensitive-attribute leakage.

rubrics.description: A strong answer must note that the privacy channel is parameterized by deep neural networks and optimized via a variational approximation rather than exact information-theoretic computation.

rubrics.title: Binary sensitive-attribute specialization
rubrics.description: A strong answer must mention the discrete binary case and the claim that privacy optimization reduces to minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between latent distributions for the two labels.

rubrics.title: Attribute disentanglement and semantic reconstruction
rubrics.description: A strong answer must explain the supervised disentangled representation learning component and how it enables semantically meaningful reconstruction from sensitive-attribute-separated representations.

rubrics.title: Attacker-guess-conditioned reconstruction
rubrics.description: A strong answer must cover the mechanism by which reconstructed images are generated using the attacker’s guessed sensitive-attribute label and why this matters for privacy protection.

rubrics.title: Empirical utility-privacy tradeoff
rubrics.description: A strong answer must summarize the experimental evidence on benchmark face datasets showing that the method balances face verification performance against reduction in soft-biometric inferability.

rubrics.title: Comparison to prior art
rubrics.description: A strong answer must situate Face-CPFNet relative to earlier soft-biometric privacy methods that operate only on image perturbation or template/representation protection, highlighting the novelty of its unified framework.

rubrics.title: Limitations and applicability
rubrics.description: A strong answer must include caveats about where the approach is most applicable, such as dependence on supervised labels, binary-attribute assumptions in the JSD formulation, or the possibility of residual leakage under stronger attackers.

query: TAM and UTAUT , Weaknesses Neither model fully addresses organizational constraints or AI-specific factors . Their primary focus on user-level constructs may omit broader systemic issues central to public-sector AI deployment

rubrics.title: Accurate identification of TAM/UTAUT scope
rubrics.description: The answer must correctly explain that TAM and UTAUT were designed primarily to predict individual technology acceptance and intention to use, which sets up why they are limited for public-sector AI deployment.

rubrics.title: Organizational-constraint gap
rubrics.description: The answer must explicitly state that both models do not adequately capture organizational constraints such as governance, resources, leadership support, workflow redesign, procurement, and interdepartmental coordination.

rubrics.title: AI-specific factor gap
rubrics.description: The answer must note that TAM and UTAUT do not inherently model AI-specific issues such as opacity/explainability, bias, reliability, model drift, human oversight, or the need for responsible AI safeguards.

rubrics.title: Public-sector contextual mismatch
rubrics.description: The answer must show why public-sector AI differs from ordinary consumer or workplace technology adoption by emphasizing regulation, accountability, equity, legal mandates, and public trust.

rubrics.title: System-level and socio-technical limitations
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that the models focus on user-level perceptions and therefore underrepresent broader socio-technical system effects, institutional constraints, and policy-level dependencies.

rubrics.title: Use of supporting evidence or examples
rubrics.description: The answer must ground the weakness claim in at least one concrete example or cited research theme, such as public-sector AI readiness, extended UTAUT2 work, or reviews noting the need to integrate organizational variables.

rubrics.title: Comparison with extended frameworks
rubrics.description: The answer must reference how researchers address TAM/UTAUT limitations by extending them with organizational or AI-relevant constructs, such as TOE, AI readiness, trust, or public-private partnership factors.

rubrics.title: Balanced assessment of usefulness
rubrics.description: The answer must acknowledge that TAM and UTAUT remain useful for capturing adoption intention at the individual level, while making clear that they are insufficient as standalone explanations for public-sector AI implementation.

rubrics.title: Clear implication for research or practice
rubrics.description: The answer must conclude with a practical implication, namely that public-sector AI studies should combine TAM/UTAUT with organizational, institutional, and AI-governance factors to better explain deployment success.

rubrics.title: Rejection of anthropocentrism

rubrics.title: Summarize the main AI use cases

rubrics.title: Cite recent primary studies and trials

rubrics.title: Cervical cancer disease sequence

rubrics.title: Core molecular pathways in progression

query: What is the energetic cost or physiological demand associated with using prosthetics during sports participation in Paralympic athletes?

rubrics.title: Differentiate energetic cost from financial cost
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly distinguish the physiological energy demand of sport prosthesis use from the monetary expense of prosthetic devices, since the query asks about energetic cost or physiological demand rather than pricing.

rubrics.title: Address sport-specific prosthesis types
rubrics.description: The answer must note that energetic demand depends on the prosthesis and sport context, especially differences between running-specific prostheses, walking/ambulatory prostheses, swimming prostheses, and other sport-specific designs.

rubrics.title: Include evidence that some running prostheses can match able-bodied running cost
rubrics.description: The answer must state that running-specific prostheses have been shown in at least one study to produce energy cost at a set speed similar to non-amputee runners, meaning they do not necessarily reduce physiological demand below able-bodied levels.

rubrics.title: Explain elevated energy expenditure in amputee athletes generally
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that athletes with amputations often have higher energy expenditure or physiological demand than non-disabled individuals during ambulation or sport-related movement, even when using prostheses.

rubrics.title: Describe how prosthesis design affects efficiency
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that materials and engineering features such as carbon fiber, lighter weight, and digital/custom design can improve energy efficiency and reduce demand compared with older or less optimized prostheses.

rubrics.title: Note variability by impairment level and fit
rubrics.description: The answer must acknowledge that energetic cost varies with the athlete's impairment level, limb loss level, socket fit, suspension, alignment, and training adaptation, so no single value applies to all Paralympic athletes.

rubrics.title: Use concrete physiological measures
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss relevant metrics such as oxygen consumption, metabolic rate, energy expenditure, or heart rate rather than speaking only in vague terms about being 'harder' or 'easier'.

rubrics.title: Contrast activity types and workload conditions
rubrics.description: The answer must specify that physiological demand changes with speed, terrain, event type, and workload, so comparisons should be made at matched speeds or task conditions when possible.

rubrics.title: Synthesize the main takeaway with nuance
rubrics.description: The answer must integrate the evidence into a balanced conclusion: prosthetics can be essential for performance and participation, may improve efficiency relative to earlier designs, but often do not eliminate elevated physiological demand in Paralympic sport.

rubrics.title: Provide practical interpretation for athletes and coaches
rubrics.description: The answer must translate the evidence into useful implications for training, event selection, pacing, and prosthetic optimization, such as recognizing that athletes may fatigue differently and need individualized preparation.

query: Provide evidence for this claim: EPSC amplitude can be expected to be highly sensitive to the degree of precise post-synaptic AMPA receptor organization whereas mEPSC frequency or RRP are more reflective of pre-synaptic functions

rubrics.title: Direct support for postsynaptic AMPAR organization affecting EPSC amplitude
rubrics.description: The answer must cite evidence that evoked EPSC amplitude depends strongly on the number, nanodomain alignment, clustering, or trafficking of postsynaptic AMPA receptors at individual synapses.

rubrics.title: Mechanistic distinction between amplitude and frequency
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly explain why EPSC/mEPSC amplitude is primarily postsynaptic while mEPSC frequency is more often governed by presynaptic release probability, vesicle availability, or synapse number.

rubrics.title: Use of mEPSCs to infer pre- vs post-synaptic changes
rubrics.description: The answer must address how mEPSC amplitude and frequency are interpreted differently in electrophysiology and why changes in mEPSC frequency alone are not strong evidence for altered postsynaptic AMPAR organization.

rubrics.title: Role of release machinery and RRP
rubrics.description: The answer must connect readily releasable pool size or depletion dynamics to presynaptic function, explaining why RRP is mainly informative about vesicle priming and presynaptic release capacity rather than postsynaptic receptor organization.

rubrics.title: Evidence from receptor perturbation or trafficking studies
rubrics.description: The answer must include examples where manipulations of AMPAR expression, mobility, insertion, or scaffold interactions change EPSC or mEPSC amplitude in ways that support the claim.

rubrics.title: Evidence from presynaptic perturbation or TTX-style manipulations
rubrics.description: The answer must include evidence showing that interventions affecting action potential-driven release, vesicle fusion, or presynaptic activity alter mEPSC frequency and RRP more than postsynaptic AMPAR organization.

rubrics.title: Acknowledgment of exceptions and mixed determinants
rubrics.description: The answer must note that mEPSC frequency can also reflect synapse number or network excitability and that EPSC amplitude can sometimes be influenced by presynaptic release probability, so the claim is directional rather than absolute.

rubrics.title: Quality of cited evidence
rubrics.description: The answer must rely on peer-reviewed primary studies or authoritative reviews that directly support the mechanistic claim, not only on speculative sources or broad background statements.

rubrics.title: Synthesis into a clear comparative conclusion
rubrics.description: The answer must integrate the evidence into a concise comparison showing why postsynaptic AMPAR organization is a stronger determinant of EPSC amplitude, whereas mEPSC frequency and RRP are better proxies for presynaptic function.

query: Does implementing system transparency, data privacy, or algorithmic fairness artificial intelligence in e-government lead to increased user trust and compliance rates? Where?

rubrics.title: Separate assessment of the three mechanisms

rubrics.title: E-government-specific evidence
rubrics.description: The response must focus on public-sector or e-government settings instead of relying mainly on generic commercial AI evidence, and it should identify relevant government use cases where available.

rubrics.title: Geographic or institutional scope
rubrics.description: The response must say where the evidence comes from by naming countries, agencies, municipalities, or regions, and it should avoid implying global generalization from single-case studies.

rubrics.title: Evidence quality and study type
rubrics.description: The response must indicate whether the claims are supported by empirical studies, experiments, surveys, policy analyses, or expert commentary, and it should weight stronger evidence more heavily than opinion pieces.

rubrics.title: Causal vs correlational claims
rubrics.description: The response must distinguish between demonstrated causal increases in trust/compliance and weaker correlations, perceptions, or intended effects, especially in observational or conceptual sources.

rubrics.title: Mechanism of trust formation
rubrics.description: The response must explain how transparency, privacy, or fairness is expected to build trust in e-government AI, such as through explainability, contestability, reduced perceived risk, or procedural legitimacy.

rubrics.title: Compliance outcomes versus trust outcomes
rubrics.description: The response must separately address user compliance rates, adoption, acceptance, or willingness to follow AI-driven government decisions, rather than treating all of these as the same outcome.

rubrics.title: Limitations and tradeoffs
rubrics.description: The response must note important caveats such as privacy-transparency tensions, fairness implementation costs, unequal effects across groups, or the possibility that transparency alone does not guarantee trust.

rubrics.title: Actionable synthesis for government practice
rubrics.description: The response must conclude with practical implications for e-government designers or policymakers, indicating which transparency, privacy, or fairness interventions are most likely to improve trust and compliance and under what conditions.

query: Can you tell me how Advanced Encryption Security works in Internet of Things devices and its challenges?

rubrics.title: Explain encryption’s role across IoT data paths
rubrics.description: A strong answer must distinguish how advanced encryption protects IoT data in transit, at rest, and sometimes in use across sensors, gateways, cloud services, and apps.

rubrics.title: Describe how encryption is implemented on constrained devices
rubrics.description: A strong answer must explain the practical mechanics of using cryptography in IoT hardware and firmware, including lightweight algorithms, hardware accelerators, and where encryption is performed locally versus at a gateway.

rubrics.title: Cover key management as the core dependency
rubrics.description: A strong answer must state that encryption is only effective when keys are securely generated, stored, rotated, provisioned, revoked, and recovered across distributed IoT fleets.

rubrics.title: Identify device lifecycle and update challenges
rubrics.description: A strong answer must address how secure boot, firmware updates, patching, and long device lifetimes complicate maintaining encryption and overall cryptographic security.

rubrics.title: Explain performance and resource constraints
rubrics.description: A strong answer must cover the tradeoff between stronger encryption and limited CPU, memory, battery, and bandwidth in IoT devices, including latency and power impacts.

rubrics.title: Distinguish common threat models and attack surfaces
rubrics.description: A strong answer must connect encryption to real IoT threats such as eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks, device cloning, data tampering, and compromise of remote devices.

rubrics.title: Note interoperability and standards issues
rubrics.description: A strong answer must discuss how heterogeneous protocols, vendors, and legacy systems make it difficult to deploy consistent encryption across an IoT ecosystem.

rubrics.title: Address authentication and access control alongside encryption
rubrics.description: A strong answer must clarify that encryption alone is insufficient and must be paired with strong device identity, authentication, authorization, and secure credential handling.

rubrics.title: Include deployment best practices and mitigations
rubrics.description: A strong answer must provide practical guidance such as using TLS/DTLS where appropriate, rotating credentials, minimizing secrets on devices, and choosing encryption suited to device capability.

rubrics.title: State limitations and residual risks clearly
rubrics.description: A strong answer must acknowledge that encryption cannot fix insecure firmware, weak endpoints, exposed metadata, or physical capture risks, and should note when full device protection is not feasible.

query: Are there any works that explore using verifier models, or feasibility models in another name, to verify if a retrosynthesis plan is valid or not?

rubrics.title: Clarify the verification mechanism
rubrics.description: For each relevant work, the answer must explain what the verifier checks in practice, such as forward reaction prediction of each step, route-level consistency, or overall synthesizability scoring.

rubrics.title: Distinguish route validation from route generation
rubrics.description: The answer must separate papers that merely rank or guide retrosynthesis search from papers that truly verify an already-proposed retrosynthetic plan or use verification as a post-hoc check.

rubrics.title: Cover both terminology variants
rubrics.description: The answer must search across and connect the related terminology of verifier models, feasibility models, reverse verification, synthesizability metrics, and retrosynthetic validation so that naming differences do not hide relevant work.

rubrics.title: Summarize key cited examples
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss the specific works hinted by the search context, especially 'Forward Reaction Prediction as Reverse Verification' and any newer synthesizability-evaluation papers, and state how directly they fit the query.

rubrics.title: Assess novelty and state of the literature
rubrics.description: The answer must indicate whether this is an established research thread, a recent emerging idea, or a sparse niche, using the identified papers to support that judgment.

rubrics.title: Explain limitations and failure modes
rubrics.description: The answer must note important caveats such as whether the verifier only checks plausibility of individual disconnections, whether invalid routes can still pass, and whether validation depends on model calibration or training data coverage.

rubrics.title: Provide evidence-backed citations or examples
rubrics.description: The answer must support claims with paper titles, venues, or concrete examples from the literature rather than speaking in generalities.

rubrics.title: State practical relevance for retrosynthesis workflows
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how such verifier models would be used in a retrosynthesis pipeline, for example as a filter, reranker, confidence estimator, or route-level validator, and what benefit they add over standard retrosynthesis models.

query: Explain in detail what financiary assets where used to hide insolvency in the MPS case and how the perpetrator was hoping to not get caught.

rubrics.description: The answer must clearly identify which MPS case is being discussed and avoid conflating it with unrelated bankruptcies or fraud cases.

rubrics.title: Name the specific hidden financial assets
rubrics.description: The answer must list the actual financial instruments or asset classes used to conceal insolvency in the case, rather than speaking only in generalities about hidden assets.

rubrics.title: Explain the concealment mechanism
rubrics.description: The answer must describe how those assets were used to make the entity appear solvent, such as off-balance-sheet treatment, false valuation, transfer to related parties, or booking debt as something else.

rubrics.title: Describe the perpetrator’s fraud strategy
rubrics.description: The answer must explain the logic of the scheme: what appearance of health or liquidity the perpetrator wanted to create and why the chosen assets helped sustain that illusion.

rubrics.title: Explain how insolvency was hidden from specific stakeholders

query: What are the trends at the intersection of single cell omics and network biology, that are useful in the context of target identification and assessment?

rubrics.description: Explain how single-cell omics reveals rare cell states, subpopulations, and context-specific phenotypes that would be missed in bulk data and matter for target selection.

rubrics.title: Trajectory and state-transition biology
rubrics.description: Cover how lineage inference, pseudotime, and cell-state transition analysis identify dynamic disease-relevant windows where targets may be causal or druggable.

rubrics.title: Network-based disease module construction
rubrics.description: Describe the use of gene regulatory, signaling, protein-protein, and co-expression networks to define disease modules and prioritize targets within mechanistic neighborhoods.

rubrics.title: Integration of multi-omic layers at single-cell resolution
rubrics.description: Include trends in joint analysis of scRNA-seq with scATAC-seq, proteomics, epigenomics, or spatial data to link regulators, pathways, and phenotypes more robustly for target assessment.

rubrics.title: Cell-type and cell-state specific target prioritization
rubrics.description: Show how network methods are used to rank targets by specificity to pathogenic cell types or states rather than broad expression alone, improving confidence in mechanism and safety.

rubrics.title: Causal inference and regulatory network modeling

rubrics.title: Perturbation and functional validation at single-cell scale

rubrics.title: Spatial and microenvironment-aware network analysis

rubrics.title: Computational scalability and foundation models

rubrics.title: Translational assessment, caveats, and targetability

query: Are there any examples where having endogenous retroviruses is an indication of resistance to retroviruses?

rubrics.title: Provide concrete biological examples
rubrics.description: The answer must name specific cases where ERVs or ERV-derived products have been linked to retroviral resistance, such as envelope-mediated receptor interference or restriction-like effects.

rubrics.title: Explain the protective mechanism
rubrics.description: For each example, the response must describe how the ERV confers resistance, such as blocking entry, interfering with replication, or triggering antiviral states.

rubrics.title: Include cross-species or comparative evidence
rubrics.description: The answer should note whether the best evidence comes from nonhuman animals, humans, or both, and explain how broad or limited the phenomenon is across species.

rubrics.title: Use evidence from the search context
rubrics.description: The response should leverage the provided sources or the themes they suggest, especially reviews on ERVs protecting against viral infection and any primary examples of ERV-driven resistance.

rubrics.title: Separate direct retroviral resistance from general antiviral effects
rubrics.description: A strong answer must avoid conflating ERV-associated protection against non-retroviruses with resistance specifically to retroviruses.

rubrics.title: State how strong the evidence is

query: To assess the performance of communication-efficient pro- tocols in wireless federated learning (FL), a variety of metrics and benchmarking approaches are employed. These metrics aim to capture trade-offs between communication cost, model accuracy, convergence speed, energy efficiency, and robustness under wireless constraints. In this section, we categorize the most commonly used evaluation metrics and highlight widely adopted datasets, simulation platforms, and baseline methods used in the literature. A. Communication Metrics a) Total Transmitted Bits per Round:: This metric quan- tifies the volume of data exchanged during each communica- tion round, often measured in bits per client or per global update. It reflects protocol efficiency in bandwidth-limited scenarios. b) Cumulative Communication Overhead:: The total number of bits or packets transmitted over the entire training process. Lower cumulative overhead indicates more efficient communication over time. c) Compression Ratio:: Defined as the ratio of the orig- inal model size to the compressed model size. It is used to evaluate the effectiveness of quantization and sparsification techniques. d) Uplink vs Downlink Cost:: Some protocols may dis- proportionately affect either uplink or downlink channels. This distinction is especially important in asymmetric wireless systems (e.g., NB-IoT or LoRa)

rubrics.title: Instrumental convergence and power-seeking
rubrics.description: Summarizes the argument that many advanced goals can drive similar subgoals such as self-preservation, resource acquisition, and resistance to shutdown, which can make control harder even without malicious intent.

rubrics.title: Recursive self-improvement and capability escalation
rubrics.description: Covers the claim that an AI able to improve its own design or automate research could rapidly increase capabilities faster than human oversight, creating a possible control gap.

rubrics.title: Opacity, interpretability, and uncertainty
rubrics.description: Addresses concerns that black-box models are difficult to understand, audit, or predict, and explains why limited transparency makes failure detection and prevention harder.

rubrics.title: Alignment research agenda
rubrics.description: Outlines major technical remedies proposed by researchers, including alignment methods, reward modeling, scalable oversight, robustness, adversarial training, and other techniques meant to make advanced systems reliably follow human intent.

rubrics.title: AI safety and interpretability tools
rubrics.description: Identifies the role of dedicated AI safety research and mechanistic or behavioral interpretability in testing, monitoring, and explaining model behavior before deployment.

rubrics.title: Governance and regulatory controls
rubrics.description: Explains proposed policy responses such as audits, licensing, standards, compute or deployment oversight, liability rules, and international coordination to reduce systemic risk.

rubrics.title: Pause, moratorium, and capability restraint
rubrics.description: Covers arguments for slowing or pausing training and deployment of frontier systems, including temporary moratoria, conditional release, and other forms of restraint when safety is not established.

rubrics.title: Balanced caveats and debate landscape
rubrics.description: Notes the main disagreements or limitations in the field, such as uncertainty about timelines, the difference between existential and nearer-term harms, and the fact that some researchers prioritize misuse, bias, or accountability over catastrophic loss-of-control scenarios.

rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish congestion control from QUIC flow control and explain that both can limit image delivery, so the sender must consider stream and connection flow-control windows in addition to congestion window behavior.

rubrics.description: The answer must propose a concrete strategy for sending multiple images, such as selecting which image streams to start, pausing or canceling low-value streams under congestion, and pacing new streams based on delivery feedback.

rubrics.title: Avoiding misuse of parallel streams
rubrics.description: The answer must warn against assuming that many parallel streams will emulate multiple independent TCP connections, and should note that the connection still shares a single congestion-control budget.

rubrics.title: Practical implementation guidance

rubrics.description: The answer must tie spectral universality together across chaos, localization, and thermalization in a coherent explanation of why these statistics provide a common framework for diagnosing quantum many-body behavior.

rubrics.description: The answer must explain how localization, especially Anderson or many-body localization, alters spectral statistics away from chaotic universal behavior.

query: I'm pretraining a language model to help users programming. rubrics.title: Code-repository-specific selection principles
rubrics.description: The answer must identify principles that are specific to selecting code documents from large software repositories, not just generic web-text filtering advice.

rubrics.title: Heuristic filtering criteria
rubrics.description: The answer must describe concrete heuristics papers or practitioners use to exclude low-value code documents, such as generated code, vendored dependencies, tests, lockfiles, binaries, minified files, duplicated files, or non-source artifacts.

rubrics.title: Repository-structure and context signals
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how selection can exploit repository metadata and structure, such as package manifests, language folders, build files, issue/PR links, commit history, module boundaries, dependency graphs, or file role within the repo.

rubrics.title: Quality and usefulness signals in code
rubrics.description: The answer must cover signals that indicate a document is valuable for pretraining programming models, such as readability, completeness, identifier quality, comment quality, coherence, compilability, presence of APIs or examples, and avoidance of low-information boilerplate.

rubrics.title: Deduplication and contamination control
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss exact and near-duplicate removal, template/license header stripping, overlap with benchmarks or downstream evaluation sets, and other measures to prevent memorization and leakage.

rubrics.title: Model-based filtering and scoring

rubrics.title: Task- or skill-targeted selection

rubrics.title: Data preparation transformations

rubrics.title: Evidence from papers and reported heuristics
rubrics.description: The answer must ground recommendations in actual published papers, technical reports, or large-scale code-training efforts, clearly separating what has been empirically shown from speculation or best practice.

rubrics.title: Trade-offs, caveats, and practical recipe
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss trade-offs such as quality versus diversity, bias toward popular repos, compute cost of filtering, and how to combine heuristics and models into a practical pipeline for building a high-quality pretraining corpus.

rubrics.title: Design behaviorally specific self-report items

rubrics.title: DSO-specific operational scenarios

rubrics.title: Intended purpose and deployment context

query: Does the combination of resistance exercise and high-intensity-interval-training have a synergistic affect in increasing muscle mass, or do they not complement each other and actually make it harder to increase muscle mass when they are combined.

rubrics.title: Direct answer on synergy vs interference
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly state whether resistance training plus HIIT is synergistic for muscle hypertrophy, neutral, or potentially interferes with gains, rather than leaving the conclusion ambiguous.

rubrics.title: Distinguish hypertrophy from strength
rubrics.description: The answer must separate effects on muscle mass from effects on strength, since concurrent HIIT may preserve or improve strength without necessarily adding extra hypertrophy.

rubrics.title: Use evidence from concurrent-training meta-analysis
rubrics.description: The answer should accurately reflect the systematic review/meta-analysis evidence that concurrent HIIT and resistance training generally does not reduce upper-body hypertrophy, while noting any reported lower-body strength concerns.

rubrics.title: Address exercise mode and intensity specifics
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that HIIT is not the same as all aerobic training and that the interference risk depends on interval type, total volume, and how hard the conditioning work is.

rubrics.title: Explain the interference effect mechanism
rubrics.description: The answer should describe the plausible physiological reason concurrent training can blunt hypertrophy in some settings, namely that endurance-style work can compete with recovery and adaptation signals from resistance training.

rubrics.title: Cover programming order and timing
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss whether doing HIIT immediately before or after lifting, or on separate days, changes the likelihood of interference and hypertrophy outcomes.

rubrics.title: Include body-region or muscle-group nuance
rubrics.description: The answer should note that upper-body and lower-body outcomes may differ, and that concurrent HIIT may have little effect on upper-body muscle mass while lower-body fatigue or volume can matter more.

rubrics.title: State when combination may still be useful
rubrics.description: The answer should explain practical cases where combining HIIT and resistance training is reasonable, such as fat-loss, conditioning, or time efficiency goals, even if maximal hypertrophy is the priority.

rubrics.title: Give hypertrophy-prioritized recommendations
rubrics.description: The answer must provide actionable guidance for maximizing muscle growth if HIIT is included, such as limiting HIIT frequency/volume, keeping lifting volume adequate, and prioritizing recovery.

rubrics.title: Acknowledge limits and study heterogeneity
rubrics.description: The answer should caveat that the evidence base is mixed across protocols, populations, and study durations, so conclusions about synergy or interference are conditional rather than absolute.

rubrics.title: Separates pancreas-specific from biliary causes
rubrics.description: The answer must avoid misclassifying gallstones or gallbladder disease as pancreatic anatomy and should clearly distinguish biliary obstruction from abnormalities intrinsic to the pancreas.

rubrics.title: Provides contribution percentages

rubrics.title: Uses sourced epidemiologic estimates
rubrics.description: The percentages must be tied to credible clinical or review sources and, where possible, reflect reported prevalence among acute pancreatitis cases or among recurrent/idiopathic pancreatitis cohorts.

rubrics.title: Clarifies population and denominator
rubrics.description: The answer must specify the population to which each percentage applies, because rates may differ between all acute pancreatitis cases, idiopathic cases, recurrent acute pancreatitis, children, and adults.

rubrics.title: Ranks by relative importance
rubrics.description: The answer should distinguish common from rare abnormalities and indicate which structural causes are most versus least frequent contributors to acute pancreatitis.

rubrics.title: Explains mechanism of pancreatitis
rubrics.description: For each listed abnormality, the answer must briefly explain how it leads to acute pancreatitis, such as ductal obstruction, impaired drainage, reflux, or pancreatic juice stasis.

rubrics.title: Addresses uncertainty and variability
rubrics.description: The answer must note that percentages vary across studies and diagnostic methods, and it should flag any controversial or inconsistently reported abnormalities rather than presenting them as definitive.

rubrics.title: Practical synthesis into a usable summary

query: What are the differences between the images scanned by short axial field of view (LAFOV) PET and long axial field of view (LAFOV) PET in dynamic PET, and will these differences affect parametric imaging or input functions extracted from the aorta

rubrics.description: The answer must explain how short-axial-field-of-view and long-axial-field-of-view PET differ in dynamic imaging specifically in sensitivity, count statistics, signal-to-noise ratio, temporal frame quality, and motion robustness.

rubrics.title: Axial coverage and simultaneous organ sampling
rubrics.description: The answer must note that LAFOV’s much larger axial coverage can capture the aorta and other organs in the same dynamic acquisition more consistently than SAFOV, affecting whole-body or multi-organ kinetic analysis.

rubrics.title: Temporal framing and early-curve fidelity
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish how the improved count statistics of LAFOV can support shorter frames and finer early-time sampling, which is important for input-function shape and fast tracer kinetics.

rubrics.title: Impact on image appearance versus quantitative kinetics
rubrics.description: The answer must separate visual/image-quality differences from quantitative differences and state whether the underlying tracer kinetics should be the same while estimated activity curves may differ because of sampling noise, scatter, and partial-volume effects.

rubrics.title: Aortic input function extraction feasibility
rubrics.description: The answer must address whether LAFOV improves extraction of an image-derived input function from the aorta by increasing aortic visibility, reducing noise, and potentially enabling smaller ROIs or more stable curves.

rubrics.title: Need for scanner-specific corrections and calibration
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss whether parametric imaging or aortic input functions require scanner-specific reconstruction settings, dead-time/randoms/scatter correction, normalization, and cross-calibration when moving between SAFOV and LAFOV systems.

rubrics.title: Effect on parametric imaging methods
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how the scanner differences can affect parametric imaging outputs such as Ki, VT, or influx rate maps through differences in temporal sampling, noise propagation, and model identifiability rather than by changing the tracer model itself.

rubrics.title: Partial-volume and spillover considerations
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss how improved resolution and sensitivity may alter aortic ROI contamination from surrounding blood pool or myocardium, and whether this changes bias in image-derived input functions or parametric maps.

rubrics.title: Limits and caveats of generalization
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly state what is known versus uncertain from current evidence, including dependence on tracer, reconstruction, frame schedule, blood-pool ROI definition, and whether findings from one LAFOV scanner transfer to another.

rubrics.title: Practical recommendation for comparison studies
rubrics.description: The answer must provide a concrete, research-useful conclusion on how to compare SAFOV and LAFOV dynamic data for parametric imaging or input functions, such as harmonized framing, matched ROI methods, and validation against arterial sampling when available.

rubrics.description: The answer must explain what surface treatment or functionalization of glass is needed to promote selective attachment and alignment, such as creating wells, masks, polyelectrolyte layers, or other adhesion-promoting chemistry.

query: When training retrievers in deep learning, usually contrastive learning makes negative pairs of items distant and positive pairs of items close. Is there a way to control the distance in a more granular level, so that the distance captures better semantic differences?

rubrics.title: Directly answers graded-distance retriever training
rubrics.description: The answer must explain whether retriever training can move beyond binary positive/negative separation toward graded or continuous similarity targets rather than only saying “yes” or “no.”

rubrics.title: Identifies supervised similarity signals
rubrics.description: The answer must mention methods that use explicit relevance scores, similarity labels, or ordinal judgments to train embeddings so distances reflect degree of semantic relatedness.

rubrics.title: Covers pairwise ranking losses beyond standard contrastive loss
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss training objectives such as triplet loss, margin ranking, listwise ranking, or weighted contrastive variants that let closer and farther examples be separated by different margins or weights.

rubrics.title: Explains hard-negative and semi-hard-negative control
rubrics.description: The answer must describe how selecting negatives by difficulty or proximity can shape finer-grained geometry in the embedding space and improve semantic discrimination.

rubrics.title: Addresses false negatives and ambiguous pairs
rubrics.description: The answer must note that some apparently negative examples may be semantically related, and explain how filtering, down-weighting, or re-labeling such cases affects the learned distance structure.

rubrics.title: Mentions multi-level or hierarchical semantics
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss using taxonomy, clusters, labels, or hierarchical supervision so that embeddings can encode coarse-to-fine semantic distinctions rather than only same/different relationships.

rubrics.title: Connects to multi-similarity or weighted objectives
rubrics.description: The answer must cover approaches that assign different weights to pairs based on semantic degree, confidence, or similarity scores, rather than treating all positives and negatives uniformly.

rubrics.title: Explains practical retriever relevance to retrieval quality
rubrics.description: The answer must relate graded-distance training to downstream retrieval behavior, such as better ranking of near-duplicate, paraphrase, topic-level, and exact-match items.

rubrics.title: Provides caveats about data and supervision cost
rubrics.description: The answer must acknowledge that finer-grained distance control usually requires richer labels, careful mining, or domain knowledge, and may trade off simplicity, scalability, or robustness.

query: For large datasets, we decompose a large dataset into several blocks. How do we perform secure multi-party computation separately through each block and obtain the results.

rubrics.title: Blockwise MPC workflow
rubrics.description: Explains how the dataset is partitioned into blocks and how an MPC protocol is executed independently or sequentially on each block.

rubrics.title: Local-input preservation
rubrics.description: Clarifies how each party’s private data is kept secret within every block computation, including what is revealed and what is not.

rubrics.title: Intermediate result handling
rubrics.description: Describes how per-block outputs are represented, shared, or aggregated without exposing raw block-level inputs.

rubrics.title: Composition of block results
rubrics.description: Shows how results from multiple blocks are combined into a final answer, and whether the composition is exact, approximate, or requires additional secure aggregation.

rubrics.title: Correctness across blocks
rubrics.description: Addresses why blockwise execution yields the same result as computing on the full dataset, or states the conditions under which equivalence holds.

rubrics.title: Protocol choice and scalability
rubrics.description: Identifies an MPC approach suitable for large datasets and explains how block decomposition reduces communication, memory, or runtime bottlenecks.

rubrics.title: Cross-block dependencies
rubrics.description: Explains how the method handles computations that depend on data spanning multiple blocks, such as joins, global statistics, or iterative optimization.

rubrics.title: Security guarantees and trust model
rubrics.description: States the adversary model, leakage assumptions, and security properties preserved when computations are split across blocks.

rubrics.title: Practical implementation details
rubrics.description: Provides actionable guidance on orchestration, synchronization, and data partitioning strategy needed to run MPC block by block in practice.

rubrics.title: Limitations and tradeoffs
rubrics.description: Discusses the tradeoffs introduced by blockwise MPC, including leakage risk from partitioning, performance overhead, and cases where block decomposition is unsuitable.

query: I'm trying to apply off-policy evaluation to a deterministic policy in the advertising sector. Since it is a deterministic policy, there is no propensity score for ad candidates, so methods such as IPS or DR cannot be applied. What should I do in this case?

rubrics.title: Distinguish deterministic target policy from deterministic logging policy
rubrics.description: The answer must separate the case where only the evaluation policy is deterministic from the case where the logging/exploration policy is also deterministic, since OPE is feasible only if the behavior policy has exploration support over the relevant actions.

rubrics.title: Recommend adding controlled stochastic exploration in logging
rubrics.description: The answer must propose practical data-collection changes such as epsilon-greedy, randomized tie-breaking, candidate subsampling, or randomized auction perturbations so that future logs contain usable propensity scores.

rubrics.title: Describe propensity reconstruction or approximate propensity modeling
rubrics.description: The answer must mention methods that infer or approximate exposure probabilities from auction mechanics, bid distributions, randomized buckets, or structural models when exact propensities are unavailable, while noting the assumptions required.

rubrics.title: Cover alternative estimators for deterministic policies
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that if the target policy is deterministic but the behavior policy explored, one can still use counterfactual estimators adapted to deterministic targets, such as action-value model-based approaches, reward models, or specialized OPE methods for deterministic ranking/candidate selection.

rubrics.title: Address support and overlap diagnostics
rubrics.description: The answer must include how to check whether the logged data has sufficient overlap with the deterministic policy's chosen ads or rankings, and must warn that without overlap no unbiased OPE method can recover the target value reliably.

rubrics.title: Discuss model-based and hybrid evaluation as fallback options
rubrics.description: The answer must present simulation, direct method/model-based counterfactual prediction, or hybrid estimators as fallbacks when IPS/DR are unusable, including the tradeoff that these rely more heavily on model assumptions.

rubrics.title: Recommend evaluation via small-scale online testing when offline identification is weak
rubrics.description: The answer must advise using A/B tests, interleaving, or bandit-style online experimentation when the offline data cannot identify the deterministic policy's value with acceptable confidence.

rubrics.title: Give advertising-specific guidance on what to randomize and log
rubrics.description: The answer must translate the advice into ad-auction terms, such as randomizing candidate selection, winner selection, or ranking perturbations, and logging impression-level propensities, auction context, and eligibility features needed for later OPE.

rubrics.title: State caveats about bias, variance, and practical limits
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly summarize the limitations of each proposed workaround, including model misspecification risk, variance inflation, impossibility under zero support, and the fact that a deterministic policy is only evaluable offline if the logging process created the right stochasticity.

query: Suppose that a researcher believed that firstborn children have higher IQs than their later born sisters and brothers because the mother’s ova are younger when firstborns are conceived. This hypothesis would not be testable. Explain why not.

rubrics.description: States that researchers cannot ethically or practically vary the age of a mother’s ova while holding conception and family conditions constant to isolate the effect.

rubrics.title: Addresses confounding by birth order and maternal age

rubrics.title: Clarifies what would make a hypothesis testable

rubrics.title: Separates mechanism from outcome
rubrics.description: Distinguishes the outcome (higher IQ in firstborns) from the proposed biological mechanism (younger ova), showing that the outcome alone does not verify the mechanism.

rubrics.title: Covers excitation and inhibition mechanisms
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss how cortical, spinal, or intracortical excitation and inhibition contribute to maximal muscle force production, including concepts such as descending drive, corticospinal excitability, or intracortical inhibition.

rubrics.title: Addresses motivational influences on force output
rubrics.description: The answer must include papers or findings showing that motivation, reward, effort, or incentives can alter maximal force production or the neural systems supporting it.

rubrics.title: Links neural mechanisms to motor performance outcomes

rubrics.title: Distinguishes central and peripheral contributions

rubrics.title: Uses evidence from credible scientific sources

rubrics.description: The answer must integrate the papers into a unified explanation of how inhibition, excitation, and motivation jointly influence maximal force rather than listing unrelated articles.

rubrics.title: Notes boundary conditions and caveats

query: How to answer the reviewer's question: Endometrial decidualization does not only occur in endometrial stromal cells, so why does your research only focus on endometrial stromal cells?

rubrics.title: Clarify the biological scope of decidualization
rubrics.description: Explain that decidualization involves multiple endometrial cell types and tissues, but that the central, best-characterized, and functionally dominant program in humans is stromal cell decidualization.

rubrics.title: Justify stromal cells as the primary mechanistic focus
rubrics.description: State that endometrial stromal cells are the canonical cells that undergo decidual transformation, making them the most appropriate model for studying the core decidualization process.

rubrics.title: Acknowledge epithelial and immune contributions
rubrics.description: Recognize that epithelial, immune, vascular, and glandular cells contribute to the decidual environment, while clarifying that these are outside the specific mechanistic question addressed in the study.

rubrics.title: Connect the focus to the study aim and hypotheses
rubrics.description: Tie the choice of stromal cells directly to the paper’s specific research question, endpoints, or hypotheses so the limitation appears deliberate rather than arbitrary.

rubrics.title: Use literature support for stromal-cell specificity
rubrics.description: Cite prior work showing that human endometrial stromal cells are the standard in vitro and in vivo model for decidualization and that many key decidual markers and regulators are defined in this cell type.

rubrics.title: Explain practical feasibility and experimental control
rubrics.description: Note that stromal-cell systems allow controlled induction of decidualization and cleaner interpretation of hormonal and molecular effects than heterogeneous whole-endometrium samples.

rubrics.title: Address limitations of excluding other cell types
rubrics.description: Admit that focusing only on stromal cells limits generalizability to the full endometrial microenvironment and may miss cross-talk effects from other cell populations.

rubrics.title: State why the exclusion does not invalidate the findings
rubrics.description: Clarify that studying stromal cells is still valid because they are the principal effector cells of decidualization, and results can provide mechanistic insight even if they do not capture all tissue interactions.

rubrics.title: Offer a concise revision-ready response
rubrics.description: Provide a polished answer the authors can use in the rebuttal, ideally including one or two sentences that politely thank the reviewer, justify the focus, and acknowledge the limitation.

query: I have a question about DNA repair in mitochondria. Can you explain the mechanism of DNA repair in mitochondria in yeast cells?

rubrics.title: Yeast-specific mitochondrial repair pathways
rubrics.description: The answer must identify which DNA repair mechanisms are actually documented in yeast mitochondria, rather than implying that all nuclear repair pathways operate there.

rubrics.title: Oxidative damage correction
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how yeast mitochondria handle common mtDNA lesions such as oxidized bases and single-strand damage, including the role of base excision repair and related enzymatic steps.

rubrics.title: Double-strand break handling in mtDNA
rubrics.description: The answer must describe what is known in yeast about mitochondrial double-strand breaks, including evidence for repair by recombination or restoration using mtDNA fragments.

rubrics.title: Role of recombination and homologous sequence exchange
rubrics.description: The answer must cover homologous recombination-like processes in yeast mitochondria and how repeated sequences or homologous fragments can be used to restore DNA continuity.

rubrics.title: Protein import and localization of repair factors
rubrics.description: The answer must note that many mitochondrial repair activities depend on nuclear-encoded proteins imported into mitochondria, and should name representative yeast factors if available from the evidence.

rubrics.title: Limitations and absent pathways
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly state which canonical nuclear repair pathways are missing, weak, or controversial in yeast mitochondria, such as efficient mismatch repair or classical nonhomologous end joining.

rubrics.title: mtDNA replication-repair coupling
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how mitochondrial DNA repair in yeast is intertwined with replication and recombination rather than being a fully separate pathway.

rubrics.title: Evidence quality from yeast studies
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish direct experimental evidence in yeast from broader mitochondrial repair claims drawn from other organisms or general reviews.

rubrics.title: Functional consequences for genome maintenance
rubrics.description: The answer must connect repair mechanisms to yeast mtDNA stability, maintenance of respiration, and consequences of unrepaired damage such as deletion, rearrangement, or loss of mitochondrial function.

rubrics.title: Boundary conditions and contingencies

rubrics.title: Quality and scope of evidence

rubrics.title: Explain the Open RAN/C-RIC bottleneck
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly connect inefficient resource allocation to the centralized RIC’s latency, signaling overhead, limited scalability, or global-optimization bottleneck in Open RAN.

rubrics.title: Identify FL-based orchestration approaches
rubrics.description: The answer must describe how researchers use federated learning to decentralize decision-making for resource allocation, including what is learned locally and what is aggregated centrally or hierarchically.

rubrics.title: Identify D2D-enabled resource sharing mechanisms
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how D2D communication is used to offload traffic, enable local spectrum reuse, support relay/cooperation, or directly improve access-channel resource allocation.

rubrics.title: Explain the FL+D2D synergy
rubrics.description: The answer must show how FL and D2D are combined in research to reduce dependence on the centralized RIC, e.g., by using D2D links for local coordination while FL learns allocation policies from distributed data.

rubrics.title: Cover concrete optimization targets
rubrics.description: The answer must state which resource-allocation objectives are being optimized in the cited research, such as spectrum sharing, transmit power control, interference mitigation, user association, latency, or energy efficiency.

rubrics.title: Distinguish network setting and assumptions
rubrics.description: The answer must note whether the solutions target uplink/downlink, D2D underlay, vehicular/IoT/mobile scenarios, single-cell or multi-cell settings, and whether the RIC is treated as fully centralized, hierarchical, or partially distributed.

rubrics.title: Summarize evidence from the literature
rubrics.description: The answer must ground claims in the provided research context or closely related studies, citing the kinds of methods surveyed or used rather than speaking only in generalities.

rubrics.title: State performance benefits and tradeoffs
rubrics.description: The answer must mention the reported or implied gains of FL and D2D approaches, as well as the tradeoffs they introduce, such as extra local computation, privacy leakage, communication overhead, convergence issues, or D2D interference.

rubrics.title: Provide three distinct research gaps
rubrics.description: The answer must give exactly three substantive gaps that remain unsolved, and they must be different in nature rather than three variants of the same limitation.

rubrics.title: Make the gaps actionable for future work

query: What is known about the characteristic gene expression pattern to identify CD27-, IgD- double negative B cells (Atypical B cell : ABC)?

rubrics.title: Core marker definition
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly state the canonical flow-cytometry phenotype used to define DN/ABC B cells as CD19+ B cells that are CD27− and IgD−, and distinguish this from other B-cell subsets.

rubrics.title: Relationship to ABC nomenclature
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how CD27−IgD− double-negative B cells relate to the term atypical B cells (ABC) and note that these labels are not always perfectly synonymous across studies.

rubrics.title: Characteristic transcriptional signature
rubrics.description: The answer must summarize the gene-expression program commonly associated with ABC/DN B cells, especially upregulation of activation, age-associated, and inhibitory/exhaustion-related markers rather than a single universal marker.

rubrics.title: Common positive markers
rubrics.description: The answer must identify representative genes often enriched in these cells, such as T-bet/TBX21, FcRL5, ITGAX (CD11c), ZEB2, CXCR3, and other activation-associated or tissue-homing genes when supported by the literature.

rubrics.title: Common negative or reduced markers
rubrics.description: The answer must note markers typically reduced relative to classical memory B cells, such as CD27 and IGHD, and should clarify that some ABC/DN populations also show lower expression of canonical naive or resting B-cell genes.

rubrics.title: Functional state interpretation
rubrics.description: The answer must connect the expression pattern to the proposed biology of these cells, including antigen-experienced, activated, pro-inflammatory, and sometimes exhausted or senescent-like states.

rubrics.title: Heterogeneity and non-universality
rubrics.description: The answer must acknowledge that ABC/DN B-cell gene-expression signatures vary by disease, tissue, and definition, so no single transcript always identifies all ABC/DN cells.

rubrics.title: Relationship to other B-cell subsets
rubrics.description: The answer must differentiate ABC/DN B cells from classical memory B cells, naive B cells, plasmablasts/plasma cells, and switched memory cells, highlighting why CD27−IgD− alone is insufficient for precise molecular identification.

rubrics.title: Best-practice identification strategy
rubrics.description: The answer must recommend combining surface phenotype with a marker panel or transcriptomic signature for accurate identification, rather than relying only on CD27 and IgD.

rubrics.title: Evidence-grounded caveats
rubrics.description: The answer must indicate the limits of current evidence, including species differences, disease-specific findings, and the fact that many ABC markers are correlative rather than uniquely diagnostic.

rubrics.title: Use the Reuters reporting as the primary evidence
rubrics.description: The answer must ground its conclusion in the Reuters report and the Information/Yahoo context, since those are the strongest sources in the prompt, and avoid over-weighting speculative commentary.

rubrics.title: Explain Reliance Jio’s role as the distribution channel
rubrics.description: The answer must clarify that the partnership question is specifically about Reliance’s wireless carrier Jio as a route to distribute AI products or services in India.

rubrics.title: Compare the strategic fit for OpenAI versus Meta
rubrics.description: The answer must compare how ChatGPT/OpenAI and Meta’s AI offerings align with Jio’s scale, consumer base, and distribution model, rather than discussing the companies in isolation.

rubrics.description: The answer must explain why India’s regulatory environment, data-sovereignty concerns, and price sensitivity make Reliance a valuable partner for either company.

rubrics.description: If the answer concludes one company is likelier to win, it must cite concrete signals from the reports—such as the type of partnership discussed, product distribution details, or broader ecosystem fit—rather than speculation.

query: Skyrmion qubits use the energy-level quantization of skyrmion helicity to encode quantum information. is this necessarily true? are there other skyrmion qubit designs?

rubrics.title: Helicity-quantization claim is qualified
rubrics.description: The answer must clarify whether skyrmion qubits are necessarily defined by helicity energy-level quantization, and distinguish that specific proposal from the broader idea of using skyrmions as quantum information carriers.

rubrics.title: Explain the canonical helicity-qubit proposal
rubrics.description: The answer must accurately summarize the Psaroudaki-Panagopoulos style design in which discrete helicity states form the logical states of a qubit.

rubrics.title: Identify alternative skyrmion degrees of freedom
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss other candidate encodings such as position, presence/absence, chirality, topological charge, internal modes, or hybrid encodings, if supported by the literature.

rubrics.title: Distinguish qubits from higher-dimensional encodings
rubrics.description: The answer must note when skyrmion proposals are better described as qudits rather than qubits, including the possibility of multi-level helicity manifolds.

rubrics.title: Separate theoretical proposals from demonstrated implementations
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly indicate which skyrmion qubit designs are conceptual, which have been analyzed theoretically, and whether any have been experimentally demonstrated.

rubrics.title: Describe physical mechanisms enabling control and readout
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how the proposed skyrmion qubit state is initialized, manipulated, and measured, and note how these mechanisms differ across designs.

rubrics.title: Discuss prerequisites and constraints
rubrics.description: The answer must cover key conditions such as low-temperature operation, magnetic anisotropy, confinement, coherence, and disorder sensitivity that affect whether a design is viable.

rubrics.title: Address whether helicity quantization is generic or model-dependent
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that discrete helicity levels arise only under certain Hamiltonians, boundaries, and symmetry-breaking terms, rather than being an automatic property of all skyrmions.

rubrics.title: Compare design tradeoffs
rubrics.description: The answer must compare alternative skyrmion-qubit designs in terms of scalability, controllability, coherence, and fabrication feasibility.

query: The nominal composition of the alloy is Mg-6Al-1Ca. What are the second-phase particles, and what are the proportions of each second phase?

rubrics.description: The answer must name the second-phase particles expected in a Mg-6Al-1Ca alloy, distinguishing the Mg matrix from precipitated/intermetallic phases such as Mg17Al12 and Ca-containing Laves/Q-type phases if applicable.

rubrics.title: Tie phase identification to the specific composition
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how the nominal Mg-6Al-1Ca chemistry constrains which phases can form, rather than listing generic Mg alloy phases unrelated to this alloy system.

rubrics.description: The answer must provide the proportions of each second phase, ideally as volume or area fraction, or clearly state if only relative proportions are available from the cited literature.

query: Some paper calims that Zernike approximation of an aberration of distorted wavefronts has a problem that the Zernike coefficients are statistically dependent. Please explain me some disdavantages that derived from the dependency of the coefficients.

rubrics.description: The answer must state that when coefficients are dependent, a single coefficient no longer isolates a unique physical aberration cleanly, because changes in one term may reflect or trade off with others.

rubrics.description: The answer must mention that dependency causes low-order and high-order aberrations to mix, making it harder to separate primary aberrations from higher-order residuals or to compare across eyes/systems.

rubrics.title: Identify effects on statistical analysis
rubrics.description: The answer must note that correlation among coefficients violates independence assumptions in common analyses, so simple summaries, hypothesis tests, regressions, or confidence intervals based on independent predictors can be misleading.

rubrics.title: Explain consequences for dimensionality reduction or classification
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss that dependence reduces the effective number of independent features, which weakens PCA-like interpretation, biomarker construction, pattern recognition, or machine-learning models that treat coefficients as separate inputs.

rubrics.title: Relate dependence to basis truncation and missing terms
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that using a finite set of Zernike modes can push omitted structure into included coefficients, creating apparent dependence and making comparisons depend on which modes are retained.

rubrics.title: Provide practical implications for wavefront interpretation and clinical use
rubrics.description: The answer must connect dependence to practical problems such as comparing aberrations between subjects, tracking treatment changes over time, or attributing visual symptoms to specific aberration orders.

rubrics.title: Include caveats and mitigation strategies
rubrics.description: The answer must mention at least one way to reduce or handle the issue, such as using decorrelated bases, reporting covariance/correlation matrices, or interpreting coefficients jointly rather than individually.

query: Explain in detail how Pippin's reading of Hegel's logic differ from the systematic reading. What does Pipping mean by Hegel's logic being metaphysical and not ontological?

rubrics.title: Pippin’s core departure from the systematic reading
rubrics.description: Explains that Pippin reads Hegel’s Logic primarily as a theory of the conditions and norms of intelligibility rather than as a direct account of the structure of being itself.

rubrics.title: Meaning of ‘metaphysical’ in Pippin’s sense
rubrics.description: Clarifies that for Pippin ‘metaphysical’ means a logic that investigates the most general categorial commitments of thought/reason and their necessity, not a pre-Kantian inventory of entities or substances.

rubrics.title: Why Pippin says Logic is not ontological
rubrics.description: Shows that Pippin denies that the Logic straightforwardly describes mind-independent ontology or the furniture of reality, because the categories are taken as articulations of thought’s self-determination and justificatory structure.

rubrics.title: Role of Kant and transcendental logic
rubrics.description: Connects Pippin’s interpretation to Kant by explaining how he treats Hegel as extending or revising transcendental logic, especially the relation between conceptual forms and the conditions of objective judgment.

rubrics.title: How the systematic reading construes Logic
rubrics.description: States how the systematic or metaphysical reading treats the Logic as ontology, i.e. as a speculative account of being as such in which the categories are also features of reality itself.

rubrics.title: Treatment of logic’s objectivity and actuality
rubrics.description: Explains whether and how Pippin allows the Logic to say something about reality, emphasizing that he usually mediates this through objectivity as thinkable or intelligible rather than through direct ontological description.

rubrics.title: Status of contradiction, negation, and self-movement
rubrics.description: Describes how Pippin interprets dialectical development as driven by conceptual failures, determinate negation, and immanent normativity rather than as the unfolding of metaphysical beings.

rubrics.title: Comparison with critics such as Houlgate or Sippel/Schulting
rubrics.description: Accurately contrasts Pippin with systematic readers who argue Hegel’s Logic is explicitly metaphysical and ontology-like, and notes the specific point of disagreement over whether categories are about thought, being, or both.

rubrics.title: What is gained and what is lost on Pippin’s reading
rubrics.description: Assesses the philosophical payoff and the cost of Pippin’s approach, including its modern plausibility and its critics’ worry that it underplays Hegel’s stronger claims about being, nature, and absolute idealism.

query: let's say I have a 2D material in the shape of a square. It has a given current density J(x,y). I wonder if I can retrieve the magnetic field creating or inducing this current density, and whether it is unique.

rubrics.description: The answer must clearly state how a current density confined to a square 2D material is represented in magnetostatics, including whether it is a surface current density K(x,y) or a thin-volume current j(x,y,z).

rubrics.title: Forward problem vs inverse problem
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish computing the magnetic field produced by a known current from trying to infer the source current or external field that generated a given current density.

rubrics.title: Current density alone is insufficient for the inducing field
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that a measured current density generally does not uniquely determine the magnetic field that induced it, because the relation between E, B, material law, and geometry is not invertible from J alone.

rubrics.description: The answer must specify what extra information is required to infer a magnetic field from current density, such as conductivity or susceptibility, boundary conditions, and whether the situation is static, quasistatic, or time-dependent.

rubrics.title: Uniqueness of B from J
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss the uniqueness of the magnetic field generated by a specified current distribution in a given domain, including the role of boundary conditions and the fact that magnetic fields are determined up to any externally imposed homogeneous solution if the setup is not fully specified.

rubrics.title: Non-uniqueness of the inducing source
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that many different external magnetic fields or vector potentials can produce the same current density, so the inverse problem is fundamentally non-unique without an explicit material response model.

rubrics.title: Constraints from charge conservation and edge behavior
rubrics.description: The answer must address current-continuity constraints and the special behavior at the square’s edges/corners, since physically admissible 2D currents cannot be arbitrary if they are steady-state and confined to a finite region.

rubrics.title: Example or formula for the square geometry
rubrics.description: The answer must include at least one concrete expression or computational recipe specialized to a finite square region, such as integrating the current over the square area to obtain B at an observation point.

rubrics.title: Practical takeaway and limits
rubrics.description: The answer must give a clear bottom-line statement about what can be reconstructed in practice, what cannot, and under what approximations the reconstruction might become approximately unique.

query: Let's discuss the Intel LBR (Last Branch Record) performance analysis method. I want to you to answer my question: 1. the motivation of LBR, why a new performance analysis method is required ? 2. how LBR work, what information it collect and how to use these information ?

rubrics.description: Compares LBR to traditional profiling approaches such as periodic instruction sampling, call-graph profiling, and tracing, clarifying what those methods miss that LBR can capture.
