rubrics.title: Depth and retention limits
rubrics.description: Notes that LBR stores only a finite number of recent branches and that older entries are overwritten, making it a sliding window rather than a full execution log.

rubrics.title: How the records are read
rubrics.description: Explains how software accesses LBR data through performance-monitoring facilities or MSR readout, typically during sampling interrupts or profiling sessions.

rubrics.title: Interpreting branch paths
rubrics.description: Shows how the recorded source-destination pairs are used to reconstruct recent control flow and identify hot paths, call chains, and branch behavior.

rubrics.title: Use cases for optimization
rubrics.description: Connects LBR data to concrete performance-analysis tasks such as branch-misprediction diagnosis, hot-path discovery, inlining decisions, and code-layout tuning.

rubrics.title: Handling advanced scenarios
rubrics.description: Mentions special uses or caveats such as analyzing indirect branches, exceptions/returns, TSX transactions, or other cases where branch history gives extra insight.

rubrics.title: Limitations and caveats
rubrics.description: Acknowledges practical constraints including sampling bias, limited history depth, overhead tradeoffs, and the fact that LBR does not by itself explain all performance problems.

query: Please provide a summary of the literature related to the use of wearable devices to estimate performance status, separately in cancer and non-cancer populations.

rubrics.title: Separate cancer and non-cancer evidence
rubrics.description: A strong answer must clearly distinguish the literature on wearable devices for estimating performance status in cancer populations from the literature in non-cancer populations rather than pooling them together.

rubrics.title: Defines performance status and its wearable proxies
rubrics.description: The answer must explain what performance status means clinically and identify the wearable-derived measures used as proxies, such as step count, activity intensity, sedentary time, gait-related metrics, or multi-sensor composite indices.

rubrics.title: Summarizes cancer-specific validation studies
rubrics.description: The answer must summarize the main cancer studies evaluating whether wearable metrics correlate with clinician-rated performance status or predict outcomes, including the types of cancers, cohorts, and study designs.

rubrics.title: Assesses strength and consistency of associations in cancer
rubrics.description: The answer must describe how strong and consistent the reported associations are between wearable metrics and performance status in cancer, noting where evidence is promising versus weak or conflicting.

rubrics.title: Explains cancer clinical utility and limitations
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss whether wearables appear useful for prognostication, treatment monitoring, or symptom burden assessment in oncology, and note practical limitations such as adherence, missing data, heterogeneity, and device validity.

rubrics.title: Summarizes non-cancer populations and target settings
rubrics.description: The answer must describe the non-cancer literature on estimating functional or performance status with wearables across relevant populations such as older adults, frailty, chronic disease, rehabilitation, or hospitalized patients.

rubrics.title: Compares non-cancer endpoints to oncology performance status
rubrics.description: The answer must clarify how non-cancer studies operationalize comparable constructs like frailty, disability, mobility, or functional capacity and how directly those outcomes map onto performance status scales used in cancer.

rubrics.title: Evaluates evidence quality and study limitations
rubrics.description: The answer must assess the quality of the literature in both domains, including sample sizes, reference standards, longitudinal versus cross-sectional designs, generalizability, and risk of bias.

rubrics.title: Identifies device and metric heterogeneity
rubrics.description: The answer must note differences across wearable platforms, sensor placement, sampling duration, analytic methods, and outcome definitions that limit cross-study comparability.

rubrics.title: Provides a synthesis of gaps and future directions
rubrics.description: The answer must conclude with the main gaps in both cancer and non-cancer evidence and specify what future studies would be needed for clinical adoption, such as standardization, external validation, and threshold development.

query: discuss and explain the relationship between blood pressure and ADHD, is there one, does there appear to be one, is there a negative correlation, is there a positive correlation or is there simply no correlation regardless of cofounders.

rubrics.title: State the direction of the observed association
rubrics.description: The answer must explicitly distinguish whether the literature points toward lower blood pressure in ADHD, higher blood pressure in ADHD, or no consistent association, rather than treating all studies as one undifferentiated signal.

rubrics.title: Separate ADHD diagnosis from ADHD symptoms
rubrics.description: The answer must note whether evidence differs for clinically diagnosed ADHD versus dimensional ADHD symptoms, since the cited studies include both and they may not imply the same relationship.

rubrics.title: Address low blood pressure findings directly
rubrics.description: The answer must explain the repeated finding in some studies that ADHD is associated with slightly lower blood pressure, including that the effect sizes are small and the association is not necessarily clinically large.

rubrics.title: Address high blood pressure/cardiovascular risk findings directly
rubrics.description: The answer must reconcile reports suggesting ADHD is linked to hypertension or broader heart-health risk by clarifying that these findings may reflect treatment effects, comorbidities, obesity, lifestyle, or ascertainment rather than a direct positive BP-ADHD correlation.

rubrics.title: Discuss confounding and adjustment
rubrics.description: The answer must evaluate how conclusions change after controlling for confounders such as age, sex, BMI/obesity, medication use, smoking, physical activity, and psychiatric comorbidity, and whether any association persists after adjustment.

rubrics.title: Distinguish correlation from causation
rubrics.description: The answer must make clear that observational associations do not establish that ADHD causes blood-pressure changes or that blood pressure causes ADHD, and it should avoid causal overstatement.

rubrics.title: Consider medication effects as a major modifier
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that stimulant ADHD medications can raise blood pressure in some patients and therefore can obscure or reverse any underlying association in treated samples.

rubrics.title: Comment on heterogeneity across populations and study designs
rubrics.description: The answer must note that findings may differ by age group, pediatric versus adult samples, national cohorts versus clinical samples, and cross-sectional versus longitudinal designs, which affects how confidently a single correlation can be claimed.

rubrics.title: Weigh the overall evidence base
rubrics.description: The answer must synthesize the cited studies into a bottom-line judgment about whether the best current evidence supports a consistent positive, negative, or near-zero correlation, and should identify that the most defensible conclusion is likely a small or inconsistent association rather than a strong universal one.

rubrics.title: Provide a practical interpretation
rubrics.description: The answer must translate the evidence into a useful takeaway, such as whether blood pressure should be routinely monitored in people with ADHD and whether clinicians should expect BP to be a reliable marker for ADHD status.

rubrics.title: Differentiate diffusion from Twitter-like models

rubrics.title: Identify empirical research gaps
rubrics.description: The answer must name concrete underexplored questions in the literature, such as cascade patterns, instance-level heterogeneity, cross-instance reach, user behavior under federation, and the role of moderation or server norms.

rubrics.title: Cover measurement and data-access limitations
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss practical obstacles to studying Mastodon diffusion, including API inconsistency, missing or partial visibility across instances, deleted content, and limits on reconstructing complete propagation graphs.

rubrics.title: Assess content, network, and community effects
rubrics.description: The answer must examine how diffusion varies by content type, network structure, community size, and instance culture, and not reduce the problem to a single generic viral-spread process.

rubrics.title: Address moderation and governance impacts
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how instance-level moderation, federation policies, defederation, and community rules shape what spreads, where it spreads, and what remains contained.

rubrics.title: Propose novel, feasible innovations

rubrics.title: Link innovation to research value

rubrics.title: Include evaluation strategy

rubrics.title: Provide actionable research directions

rubrics.title: Christian Holy Week context

rubrics.title: Catholic historical practice
rubrics.description: The answer must describe Catholic sources and practice, including whether any liturgical or devotional tradition historically discouraged work on Good Friday and how that relates to the laundry taboo.

rubrics.title: Protestant and reformation-era attitudes
rubrics.description: The answer must address how different Protestant traditions treated Holy Week observance and whether the laundry prohibition appears more as inherited folk piety than as a theological requirement.

rubrics.title: Orthodox and Eastern Christian customs
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss any Eastern Orthodox or other Eastern Christian customs around Holy Week labor restrictions, noting where abstaining from laundry reflects fasting discipline, grief, or household preparation rather than a universal rule.

rubrics.title: Regional folk-belief origins
rubrics.description: The answer must trace the prohibition in at least a few specific regions or cultures where it is documented as a superstition or omen, rather than presenting it as a single global Christian tradition.

rubrics.title: Symbolic meanings of water, death, and purification
rubrics.description: The answer must explain the symbolic logic behind the taboo, such as associating washing with disrespect during Christ's passion, fear of bad luck, or beliefs about cleansing and sacred time.

rubrics.title: Role of household labor and Sabbath-like rest
rubrics.description: The answer must connect the laundry ban to broader historical restrictions on domestic work during holy days, including ideas of rest, reverence, and avoiding noisy or mundane tasks in sacred time.

rubrics.title: Evidence quality and uncertainty
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish well-attested historical evidence from modern blog, forum, or social-media claims, and explicitly note where the origin is unclear or contested.

rubrics.title: Practical cross-tradition summary
rubrics.description: The answer must end with a concise comparison showing which traditions genuinely forbid laundry, which merely discourage it, and which treat it as harmless, so the reader can apply the result across traditions.

rubrics.title: Use evidence from article descriptions or abstract-level claims

query: You study an Archaea living in extreme environmental conditions using combined genomic and transcriptomic approaches. After thorough data analysis, you discovered a target gene, which may be related to the tolerance of your organism to harsh environmental conditions. However, the specific molecular function of this gene is unknown. Which strategy should you choose to reveal the exact function of the gene? Choices: (A) study an organism with diminished transcriptional activity or an amplified number of pre-mRNAs of a target gene (B) study an organism using RNA interference mechanism for target gene to obtain gain-of-function phenotype (C) study an organism using CRISPR-Cas9 constructions with an inactive endonuclease fused with a green fluorescent protein (D) study a wild-type organism and estimate the expression of a target gene under a range of environmental conditions

rubrics.title: Identify the perturbation-based functional strategy
rubrics.description: A strong answer must recommend a loss- or gain-of-function perturbation approach rather than mere correlation to determine the gene’s exact role.

rubrics.title: Reject expression-only inference
rubrics.description: A strong answer must explain that measuring the target gene’s expression across environmental conditions can suggest involvement in stress response but cannot reveal the precise molecular function.

rubrics.title: Select the correct option from the choices
rubrics.description: A strong answer must explicitly choose option C as the best strategy among the four provided.

rubrics.title: Explain why CRISPR-based targeting is appropriate
rubrics.description: A strong answer must note that CRISPR-based manipulation is the relevant modern tool for testing gene function in archaea, especially when combined with reporter or imaging constructs.

rubrics.title: Flag the inactive endonuclease nuance
rubrics.description: A strong answer must recognize that an endonuclease-inactive Cas9 fused to GFP is primarily a DNA-binding/localization or visualization tool, not a direct knockout, and should relate this limitation to functional inference.

rubrics.title: Discuss why the other options are biologically mismatched
rubrics.description: A strong answer must briefly reject RNA interference in archaea and the pre-mRNA/transcriptional activity option as inappropriate for revealing exact gene function in this context.

rubrics.title: Link function discovery to stress tolerance
rubrics.description: A strong answer must connect the gene-discovery strategy to the organism’s adaptation to harsh environmental conditions, showing how perturbation under stress can expose phenotype-function relationships.

rubrics.title: Distinguish molecular function from expression pattern
rubrics.description: A strong answer must make clear that knowing when a gene is induced under stress does not by itself identify what biochemical or cellular activity the gene performs.

rubrics.title: State the experimental logic for validation
rubrics.description: A strong answer must describe that a valid function-revealing strategy would compare phenotypes and/or molecular readouts after targeted gene disruption or repression versus appropriate controls.

query: In Empire of Cotton, the historian Beckert argues that cotton textile manufacturers and their financiers were dictating British foreign policy and supporting slavery in cotton growing areas from the 1800s to the end of the Civil War and beyond. Is he correct?

rubrics.title: Assess evidence for policy influence
rubrics.description: The answer must evaluate whether there is concrete historical evidence that textile manufacturers and financiers exercised significant leverage over British diplomatic or imperial decisions, rather than merely sharing interests with policymakers.

rubrics.title: Check chronology and scope
rubrics.description: The answer must address whether Beckert’s claim is meant to apply across the entire 1800s, the U.S. Civil War period, and the postwar era, noting that British policy and cotton-market dynamics changed over time.

rubrics.title: Distinguish support for slavery from dependence on slave cotton
rubrics.description: The answer must separate the claim that British firms economically benefited from slave-produced cotton from the stronger claim that they actively supported slavery as a political project.

rubrics.title: Use concrete historical examples
rubrics.description: The answer must cite specific episodes, actors, or policies—such as the Lancashire cotton crisis, blockade-running, recognition debates, or British imperial interventions in cotton-growing regions—to substantiate or challenge Beckert’s argument.

rubrics.title: Consider counterevidence and alternative explanations
rubrics.description: The answer must weigh competing explanations for British foreign policy, including strategic, geopolitical, humanitarian, anti-slavery, and broader imperial motives that may have limited or overridden cotton interests.

rubrics.title: Evaluate the claim of 'dictating' foreign policy

rubrics.title: Account for financial-sector role separately from manufacturers
rubrics.description: The answer must analyze financiers as a distinct group from textile manufacturers, since their exposure to trade disruption, credit, and imperial policy may have differed and should not be treated as a single unified lobby.

rubrics.title: Address empire and coercion beyond slavery
rubrics.description: The answer must note whether Beckert’s argument about support for slavery extends to broader imperial coercion in cotton-growing regions such as India, Egypt, or other colonies, and how that bears on the British case.

rubrics.title: Give a nuanced bottom-line judgment
rubrics.description: The answer must end with a clear, qualified verdict on whether Beckert is correct overall, specifying which parts of his claim are well supported, overstated, or unsupported.

rubrics.title: Explain training data and supervision sources

rubrics.title: Explain reinforcement learning and verification

rubrics.title: Note limitations and tradeoffs
rubrics.description: Address key caveats such as higher latency, greater compute cost, possible hallucinated reasoning traces, and the fact that more visible reasoning does not guarantee better correctness.

rubrics.title: Give practical guidance for users

rubrics.title: Explain the treatment strategy and timing
rubrics.description: The answer must describe how the immune modulators were administered relative to antiretroviral therapy and interruption of medication, since timing is central to the effect.

rubrics.title: Clarify whether other therapies were part of the protocol
rubrics.description: The answer must state whether the long-term effect depended on antiretrovirals, vaccines, latency-reversing agents, broadly neutralizing antibodies, or other co-interventions in addition to immune modulators.

rubrics.title: Report the actual response rate and endpoint definition
rubrics.description: The answer must quantify the roughly 20% result accurately and explain what endpoint was measured, such as sustained undetectable viral load after treatment interruption.

rubrics.title: Describe evidence quality and trial stage

rubrics.title: Summarize mechanism of action in plain terms

rubrics.title: Include caveats about durability, generalizability, and safety
rubrics.description: The answer must note limitations such as small sample size, relapse risk, incomplete understanding, adverse effects, and whether the result is applicable to broader patient populations.

rubrics.title: Provide a direct, practical bottom-line answer

query: Some plant foods have anti-nutrients that might hamper the absorption of protein, what's the ideal way to circumvent it?

rubrics.title: Clarify the actual concern
rubrics.description: Explain that anti-nutrients generally do not prevent protein absorption outright, but can reduce digestibility or mineral absorption depending on the food and preparation method.

rubrics.title: Identify the main relevant anti-nutrients
rubrics.description: Name the key compounds in plant foods that are most relevant to protein-related concerns, especially protease inhibitors and tannins, while distinguishing them from phytates and other anti-nutrients that mainly affect minerals.

rubrics.title: Differentiate by food type
rubrics.description: Address that the ideal mitigation depends on whether the food is legumes, grains, nuts, or seeds, since anti-nutrient profiles and effective preparation methods vary by category.

rubrics.title: Recommend the most effective preparation methods
rubrics.description: State the best-supported ways to reduce anti-nutrients—soaking, sprouting/germination, fermenting, and thorough cooking or pressure cooking—and explain that heat is especially important for inactivating protein-digesting enzyme inhibitors.

rubrics.title: Explain which methods work best for protein availability
rubrics.description: Go beyond generic anti-nutrient reduction and specify that combining soaking plus cooking, or sprouting plus cooking, is often most practical for improving digestibility and protein accessibility in legumes and grains.

rubrics.title: Include practical food-specific examples
rubrics.description: Provide concrete examples such as beans/lentils needing soaking and boiling or pressure cooking, and grains or seeds benefiting from soaking, sprouting, or fermentation, so the advice is actionable.

rubrics.title: Address balancing nutrient retention and safety
rubrics.description: Discuss the tradeoff that some methods reduce anti-nutrients but can also affect other nutrients or texture, and note that adequate cooking is essential for safety in foods like beans.

rubrics.title: Distinguish protein from mineral absorption effects
rubrics.description: Make clear that phytates are more strongly linked to reduced iron, zinc, and calcium absorption than to protein absorption, so the answer should not overstate protein-specific harm.

rubrics.title: Assess the role of dietary diversity and protein quality
rubrics.description: Explain that overall protein adequacy depends on total intake, amino acid completeness, and food variety, and that anti-nutrient reduction is only one part of optimizing plant protein nutrition.

rubrics.title: Give a realistic bottom-line recommendation
rubrics.description: Conclude with a practical hierarchy of what most people should do—use properly cooked legumes and grains, prefer soaking/sprouting/fermentation when convenient, and prioritize overall diet quality rather than avoiding plant foods.

query: Dynamic programming requires: A) Sampled transitions B) Neural network approximations C) A complete model of the environment D) Model-free updates

rubrics.title: Why sampled transitions are not required

rubrics.title: Why neural networks are not required
rubrics.description: The answer must make clear that neural network approximations are optional in approximate dynamic programming and are not a requirement of dynamic programming itself.

rubrics.title: Why model-free updates are incorrect
rubrics.description: The answer must explicitly reject option D by noting that model-free updates are associated with methods like Q-learning or SARSA, not dynamic programming.

rubrics.title: Complete environment model meaning

rubrics.title: Contrast with RL methods in context
rubrics.description: The answer must situate DP relative to reinforcement learning by contrasting it with methods that learn from interaction without a full environment model.

rubrics.title: Concise justification of the choice
rubrics.description: The answer must provide a short reasoning chain showing why C is the only correct choice among the four options.

rubrics.title: Optional caveat on approximate DP
rubrics.description: If the answer mentions approximate dynamic programming, it must clarify that approximation techniques can be used to scale DP but do not change the fact that classical DP assumes access to a model.

query: systemd-journald crashed with sigabrt in __GI_fsync(). Ubuntu is installed on an external HDD. Ubuntu is restarted and because in the BIOS the internal HDD is the default booting device, the system starts the Windows OS installed on it. This is what I intend to when selecting restart on Ubuntu, but it looks like Ubuntu doesn't like it. What can be done to avoid that ?

rubrics.title: Identify the real cause: journald abort from fsync/I/O hang
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that the SIGABRT in __GI_fsync() is likely a symptom of stalled or failing disk I/O during shutdown/restart, not simply that Ubuntu "doesn't like" booting Windows.

rubrics.title: Connect the external-HDD setup to the failure mode
rubrics.description: The answer must explicitly relate Ubuntu being installed on an external HDD to shutdown/restart behavior, including the possibility that the external drive is still busy or slow to flush data when reboot is initiated.

rubrics.title: Explain why rebooting to a BIOS-selected Windows disk can trigger the issue
rubrics.description: The answer must describe how a reboot that changes the boot target to the internal Windows disk can leave the Ubuntu system or external disk in an unexpected state while systemd-journald is still trying to sync logs.

rubrics.title: Distinguish normal reboot from hard power loss or unsafe device removal
rubrics.description: The answer must make clear whether this is equivalent to unplugging or powering off the external Ubuntu disk too early, and why that matters for journald and filesystem consistency.

rubrics.title: Provide concrete mitigation steps for a clean shutdown/restart
rubrics.description: The answer must suggest practical ways to ensure Ubuntu fully shuts down before booting Windows, such as waiting for complete power-off, avoiding immediate reboot, or using a proper shutdown sequence rather than an abrupt reset.

rubrics.title: Address BIOS/UEFI boot-order limitations and user expectations
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that BIOS default boot order controls which OS starts after restart, and that if Windows is intended after Ubuntu shutdown, Ubuntu cannot guarantee a restart into Windows unless the boot path is managed deliberately.

rubrics.title: Recommend safer boot-selection methods when using dual-boot across disks
rubrics.description: The answer must propose alternatives such as using the firmware boot menu, changing the one-time boot entry, or using bootloader/UEFI settings to select Windows without leaving Ubuntu in an unstable shutdown path.

rubrics.title: Consider external drive reliability, cabling, and power issues
rubrics.description: The answer must mention that external HDDs are more prone to timing, power, USB enclosure, or cable issues that can cause fsync hangs, and suggest checking SMART, cables, ports, and enclosure reliability.

rubrics.title: Include diagnostic and logging guidance when the problem persists
rubrics.description: The answer must suggest where to look for corroborating evidence, such as journal logs, shutdown messages, I/O errors, or filesystem errors, to confirm whether the crash is caused by disk latency or hardware problems.

rubrics.title: Offer a balanced caveat if the behavior may be a known systemd bug
rubrics.description: The answer must acknowledge that journald aborts in fsync() have been reported as systemd bugs in some contexts, while still emphasizing that the external-HDD shutdown/reboot pattern is the key factor to fix first.

query: what is the difference between Value Network, Policiy Network and Q-learning in Reinforcement Learning

rubrics.title: Correctly distinguishes value, policy, and action-value functions
rubrics.description: The answer must define value networks as approximating V(s), policy networks as approximating π(a|s), and Q-learning as learning Q(s,a), not conflating these different targets.

rubrics.title: Explains the role of each in decision-making
rubrics.description: The answer must state that value networks estimate how good a state is, policy networks directly choose actions, and Q-learning uses learned action values to derive a policy such as greedy action selection.

rubrics.title: Clarifies model-free reinforcement learning framing
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that all three commonly appear in model-free RL, but Q-learning is an algorithm, while value network and policy network are neural-network function approximators that can be used within different RL algorithms.

rubrics.title: Separates actor and critic concepts
rubrics.description: The answer must note that policy networks correspond to the actor, value networks often serve as the critic, and Q-learning can be viewed as learning an action-value critic without an explicit separate actor.

rubrics.title: Describes on-policy vs off-policy differences
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that standard Q-learning is off-policy, while many policy-gradient methods using policy networks are on-policy, and it should connect this difference to how data is collected and used.

rubrics.title: Explains how learning signals differ
rubrics.description: The answer must compare the update targets: value networks learn from returns or bootstrapped value targets, policy networks learn from gradients of expected return, and Q-learning learns toward Bellman targets using reward plus discounted future Q-values.

rubrics.title: Compares action-selection behavior and action-space suitability
rubrics.description: The answer must mention that policy networks can naturally handle stochastic and continuous action spaces, whereas vanilla Q-learning is typically most straightforward in discrete action spaces because it selects among enumerated actions.

rubrics.title: Notes exploration and stability tradeoffs
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss practical differences such as Q-learning’s need for exploration strategies like epsilon-greedy and its bootstrapping instability, versus policy networks’ direct stochastic exploration and value networks’ role in reducing variance or stabilizing training.

rubrics.title: Provides a concrete comparison or example
rubrics.description: The answer must include a small example or table showing how each method would behave in a simple environment, such as choosing among discrete actions or evaluating a state, to make the distinctions operational.

rubrics.title: Avoids conflating architectures with algorithms and includes caveats
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly state that 'network' refers to a function approximator and that value/policy networks are not standalone algorithms, while also noting common hybrid methods like actor-critic and DQN that combine these ideas.

query: Consider a market in which two identical firms (A and B) provide a homogeneous good. The firms can collude and charge a higher price or they can charge a competitive price. If they agree to collude, each earns 3 units of money per month. If one of the firms sets a collusive (higher) price and the other a competitive price, the firm with the lower price earns 4 units and the one with the higher price makes a loss of 1 unit. rubrics.title: Accurate payoff matrix
rubrics.description: The answer must assign the four outcome payoffs exactly as stated: (collude, collude) gives (3,3), (collude, competitive) gives (-1,4), (competitive, collude) gives (4,-1), and (competitive, competitive) gives (0,0).

rubrics.title: Clear interpretation of labels
rubrics.description: The answer must make clear which strategy corresponds to the high-price collusive action and which corresponds to the competitive low-price action, so the matrix entries are not ambiguous.

rubrics.title: Best-response analysis for both firms
rubrics.description: The answer must analyze each firm's best response to the other's possible action and show why a firm prefers competitive pricing when the rival colludes and also when the rival is competitive.

rubrics.title: Identification of pure-strategy Nash equilibrium
rubrics.description: The answer must identify the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium as both firms choosing the competitive price and justify that neither firm can profitably deviate unilaterally from this outcome.

rubrics.title: Exclusion of collusive outcome as equilibrium
rubrics.description: The answer must explain why mutual collusion is not a Nash equilibrium despite yielding 3 each, namely because either firm can deviate to competitive pricing and increase its payoff to 4.

rubrics.title: Mutual deviation logic
rubrics.description: The answer must note that the asymmetric outcomes are not equilibria because the firm earning -1 would deviate to competitive pricing, preventing any one-sided collusive outcome from being stable.

rubrics.title: Game-theoretic classification
rubrics.description: The answer should recognize the structure as a prisoner's-dilemma-style payoff matrix in which competitive pricing is a dominant strategy for both firms and the cooperative outcome is payoff-superior but unstable.

rubrics.title: Concise but complete conclusion
rubrics.description: The answer must end with a direct statement of the equilibrium profile and its payoff, making the final result easy to verify and use.

query: I have two samples drawn from a distribtion H - The human distribution and M - The model distribution. I want to get the distance between H and M using the Wasserstein distance. To interprete the distance, I want to bootstrap on H for N times to calculate the mean distance between two bootstrap version of H. If the distance between M and the mean distance between H, I want to accept the distributions as about the same. Is this valid and has somebody done something similar?

rubrics.title: Correctly frames the null hypothesis
rubrics.description: The answer must state that the relevant question is whether H and M can be treated as samples from the same underlying distribution, not whether the observed Wasserstein distance is small in an absolute sense.

rubrics.title: Explains the bootstrap reference distribution
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that bootstrapping H and comparing H-to-H Wasserstein distances is a way to estimate the sampling variability of the distance statistic under a same-distribution null or pseudo-null, rather than a direct proof of equality.

rubrics.title: Addresses the asymmetry of the proposed comparison
rubrics.description: The answer must note that bootstrapping only H may be insufficient because the variability of the Wasserstein distance depends on both sample sizes and both empirical distributions, so a more defensible calibration may require resampling from both H and M or a pooled/permutation-style null.

rubrics.title: Clarifies what decision rule is statistically valid
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish between comparing M to the mean bootstrap H-H distance and using a threshold based on the full bootstrap distribution, and it should explain that a mean alone is generally not an appropriate acceptance criterion.

rubrics.title: Discusses hypothesis testing versus equivalence
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that 'accept the distributions as about the same' is an equivalence or non-inferiority claim, which requires an explicit tolerance or equivalence margin rather than simply failing to reject a difference test.

rubrics.title: Explains dependence on sample size and dimension
rubrics.description: The answer must address that Wasserstein distances and their bootstrap distribution depend strongly on sample size and dimensionality, so any interpretation must calibrate against n, d, and possibly scaling/normalization choices.

rubrics.title: Mentions alternative and more standard tests
rubrics.description: The answer must identify related methods such as permutation tests, bootstrap-based two-sample tests, MMD, energy distance, or Wasserstein-based two-sample tests as more established ways to compare distributions.

rubrics.title: Cites relevant prior work or analogous methods
rubrics.description: The answer must mention whether similar approaches have been studied, including Wasserstein-based bootstrap or double-bootstrap testing literature, and should distinguish direct support from merely related transport-distance work.

rubrics.title: Gives a practical implementation recipe
rubrics.description: The answer must provide a concrete procedure for calibrating the Wasserstein statistic under the null, including how to resample, what statistic to compute, how to obtain a p-value or threshold, and how to decide equivalence.

rubrics.title: States caveats about interpretation and power
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss limitations such as small-sample noise, sensitivity to support mismatch and scaling, and the possibility that a bootstrap-based rule may have low power or misleading calibration if used without formal testing.

query: When using C-Space for path planning with a mobile robot or arm, is there any example of building a perfect C-Space with a preliminary map and updating the configuration space only with the difference between the newly created map and the preliminary map during operation?

rubrics.title: Direct answer on existence of incremental C-space examples
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly state whether published examples exist of building an initial or complete C-space from a preliminary map and then updating only the changed portion when new map data arrives.

rubrics.title: Distinguish exact C-space maintenance from workspace map updates
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish between incrementally updating a workspace occupancy map and incrementally updating the derived configuration-space obstacles, since these are not the same operation.

rubrics.title: Describe known incremental or dynamic motion-planning approaches
rubrics.description: The answer must identify relevant families such as dynamic replanning, incremental collision checking, or replanning methods that reuse prior search results, and explain whether they actually maintain a C-space difference update.

rubrics.title: Explain applicability to mobile robots versus manipulators
rubrics.description: The answer must compare how feasible the idea is for mobile bases versus robotic arms, noting that arm C-spaces are high-dimensional and usually harder to update explicitly than map-based 2D/3D cases.

rubrics.title: Use of map-delta or local obstacle change propagation
rubrics.description: The answer must discuss whether and how obstacle changes in the workspace can be propagated only locally into the C-space, including any conditions under which convolution or Minkowski-sum changes remain local.

rubrics.title: Cite concrete examples or literature if available
rubrics.description: The answer must provide specific algorithm names, papers, systems, or benchmarks that demonstrate incremental C-space construction, dynamic obstacle handling, or closely related behavior rather than speaking only in generalities.

rubrics.title: Clarify computational tradeoffs and why full recomputation is common
rubrics.description: The answer must explain why many systems recompute collision checks or update planning graphs instead of maintaining a perfect global C-space, including dimensionality, complexity, and memory tradeoffs.

rubrics.title: Address exactness versus approximation
rubrics.description: The answer must state whether the approach is exact or approximate, and if it is approximate, explain what is lost compared with a true updated C-space representation.

rubrics.title: Provide practical implementation guidance
rubrics.description: The answer must suggest a realistic architecture for using a preliminary map with incremental updates in practice, such as map update plus collision/query cache plus replanning, and indicate what part of the pipeline would be updated from differences.

rubrics.title: Separate treatment of pore type and morphology
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish blowholes from closed pores and discuss how size, shape, distribution, connectivity, and location relative to grain boundaries change their creep impact.

rubrics.title: Grain-boundary liquid phase role
rubrics.description: The answer must analyze the grain-boundary liquid phase as a high-temperature weakening factor or, where applicable, as a phase that can alter diffusion and sliding, including when a thin liquid film accelerates creep versus when a beneficial boundary phase may improve resistance.

rubrics.title: Temperature and stress dependence
rubrics.description: The answer must describe how the influence of all three features changes with temperature, applied stress, and creep stage, rather than presenting a single fixed effect.

rubrics.title: Quantitative creep-law linkage

rubrics.title: Damage evolution and failure modes
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how these defects contribute to creep damage accumulation and fracture paths, including cavity nucleation, intergranular cracking, coalescence, and rupture initiation.

rubrics.title: Material class and microstructure dependence
rubrics.description: The answer must note that the influence law differs across materials such as cast alloys, powder metallurgy parts, ceramics, or superalloys and depends on grain size, boundary character, and matrix strength.

rubrics.title: Relative severity ranking
rubrics.description: The answer must provide a reasoned comparison of whether blowholes, closed pores, or grain-boundary liquid phase are typically most harmful to creep performance and under what conditions that ranking can change.

rubrics.title: Evidence-grounded synthesis
rubrics.description: The answer must synthesize findings from the provided literature context or comparable high-temperature creep studies and clearly separate well-supported conclusions from inference or uncertainty.

query: What are the clearest references on the thresholds for no rehashing (with high probability) for cuckoo hashing.

rubrics.title: Defines the exact “no rehashing” threshold question
rubrics.description: The answer must clearly distinguish the offline/insert-all-at-once cuckoo hashing threshold from online insertion failures that trigger rehashing, and specify that the query is about the asymptotic load/density threshold with high probability.

rubrics.title: States the best-known threshold values
rubrics.description: The answer must report the clearest threshold formula(s) for cuckoo hashing, including the classic 2-choice case and the general k-choice case, rather than only giving a qualitative statement that a threshold exists.

rubrics.title: Connects threshold to the underlying random graph/hypergraph model
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that failure/no-rehashing thresholds are characterized by the emergence of a giant complex component or 2-core/peeling threshold in the associated random graph or hypergraph model.

rubrics.title: Cites the main tight-threshold reference
rubrics.description: The answer must identify Dietzfelbinger and Goerdt’s ‘Tight Thresholds for Cuckoo Hashing via XORSAT’ as the key reference for exact thresholds and indicate what problem it resolves.

rubrics.title: Includes the sharp-load-threshold reference
rubrics.description: The answer must mention the complementary ‘Sharp Load Thresholds for Cuckoo Hashing’ reference and explain how it relates to the threshold statement or strengthens the asymptotic result.

rubrics.title: Explains the role of high probability
rubrics.description: The answer must state precisely what ‘with high probability’ means in this setting, namely that the probability of successful placement without rehashing tends to 1 below the threshold and tends to 0 above it as n grows.

rubrics.title: Separates 2-choice from k-choice behavior
rubrics.description: The answer must note whether the threshold depends on the number of hash choices and, if so, explain that the reference result covers all k>2 and how the 2-choice case differs or is treated in the literature.

rubrics.title: Gives a practical threshold interpretation
rubrics.description: The answer must translate the threshold into a usable load-factor limit or occupancy ratio that practitioners can use to estimate when rehashing becomes likely.

rubrics.title: Summarizes proof technique at a high level
rubrics.description: The answer must briefly explain the proof idea used in the key references, such as the reduction to XORSAT and the connection to satisfiability/2-core thresholds, enough to justify why the cited references are authoritative.

rubrics.title: Flags scope and caveats
rubrics.description: The answer must clarify any limits of the cited results, such as whether they apply to offline construction, ideal random hash functions, asymptotics, and not necessarily to finite-size or adversarial settings.

query: What is the derivative of the resistance distance with respect to the local resistance or conductivity on an electrical network, with references?

rubrics.description: The answer must clearly distinguish resistance distance/effective resistance from ordinary branch resistance and state which quantity is being differentiated with respect to local resistance or local conductivity.

rubrics.title: Graph/Laplacian formulation
rubrics.description: The answer must express resistance distance in terms of the weighted graph Laplacian or its pseudoinverse, since the derivative depends on this network formulation.

rubrics.title: Edge-resistance derivative formula
rubrics.description: The answer must give the explicit derivative of effective resistance between two nodes with respect to a single edge resistance, including the standard formula in terms of current-flow or voltage-drop along that edge.

rubrics.title: Conductivity derivative via chain rule
rubrics.description: The answer must convert the resistance derivative into a conductivity derivative using the relation between edge resistance and conductance, and state the sign change and scaling factor correctly.

rubrics.title: Dependence on source-target pair
rubrics.description: The answer must explain that the derivative depends on the chosen node pair and on whether the perturbed edge lies on, near, or far from the dominant current paths between them.

rubrics.title: General network sensitivity result
rubrics.description: The answer must include the broader sensitivity identity for effective resistance on a weighted network, not just a special-case series or parallel circuit example.

rubrics.title: Reference to classical literature
rubrics.description: The answer must cite at least one classical or foundational source on resistance distance or effective resistance sensitivity, such as Klein and Randić, Doyle and Snell, or related graph-theoretic electrical network literature.

rubrics.title: Reference to physics or percolation literature
rubrics.description: The answer must cite a source connecting local conductivity/resistivity derivatives in disordered or percolative networks to effective network response, such as the percolation and conduction reference in the search context.

rubrics.title: Assumptions and caveats
rubrics.description: The answer must state the assumptions under which the derivative formula holds, including connected network, linear ohmic elements, and whether edge weights are fixed or all other edges are held constant.

rubrics.title: Practical computation or interpretation
rubrics.description: The answer must explain how the derivative can be computed or interpreted in practice, for example via solving one network problem for the relevant node potentials or current flow rather than differentiating the full pseudoinverse directly.

query: Rural populations in Mecklenburg County, representing approximately 3.2% of the county's total population, face distinct challenges in maternal healthcare despite the county's overall urban character. rubrics.description: The answer must include sources showing that many existing DMH interventions, chatbots, screening tools, or apps are built on Western assumptions or data and may not transfer well to Indian users.

rubrics.title: Cover design implications for localization and adaptation
rubrics.description: The answer must explain what cultural tailoring would require in practice, such as language, tone, family involvement, privacy concerns, stigma-sensitive onboarding, and context-aware content.

rubrics.title: Include evidence on engagement barriers and acceptance concerns
rubrics.description: The answer must summarize findings on why Indian young adults may not use or trust DMH tools, including fears about confidentiality, low perceived relevance, stigma, usability, and lack of contextual fit.

rubrics.title: Separate empirical findings from design recommendations
rubrics.description: The answer must distinguish between articles that provide direct user evidence or study results and articles that offer speculative or proposed design principles.

rubrics.title: Assess the strength and relevance of each cited article
rubrics.description: The answer must indicate which articles are strongest for demonstrating the gap, and why, based on study population, methodology, and closeness to Indian young-adult experiences.

rubrics.title: Synthesize across sources into a coherent literature gap statement
rubrics.description: The answer must integrate the articles into a concise argument showing that the literature supports a real gap in culturally and socially attuned DMH tools for Indian young adults, not just isolated concerns.

query: Study on the association between sulfonamides, macrolides, β - lactams, tetracyclines, quinolones, lincolamines, and chloramphenicol antibiotics and gut microbiota

rubrics.title: Class-specific coverage
rubrics.description: The answer must address each requested antibiotic class—sulfonamides, macrolides, β-lactams, tetracyclines, quinolones, lincolamines, and chloramphenicol—rather than treating antibiotics as a single undifferentiated exposure.

rubrics.title: Direction of association
rubrics.description: The answer must state how antibiotic exposure affects gut microbiota for each class, including whether the association is with reduced diversity, compositional shifts, depletion of beneficial taxa, overgrowth of opportunists, or recovery after cessation.

rubrics.title: Comparative strength and persistence
rubrics.description: The answer must compare the magnitude and duration of microbiota disruption across classes, highlighting which antibiotic groups appear more disruptive or longer-lasting than others.

rubrics.title: Mechanistic interpretation
rubrics.description: The answer must explain plausible mechanisms linking these antibiotics to microbiota changes, such as broad-spectrum killing, selective pressure, resistance selection, and downstream metabolic or ecological effects.

rubrics.title: Human evidence and study types
rubrics.description: The answer must ground claims in human data where available and distinguish findings from cohort studies, longitudinal follow-up, controlled trials, and reviews rather than relying only on animal or in vitro evidence.

rubrics.title: Taxonomic and functional outcomes
rubrics.description: The answer must describe not only compositional shifts but also functional consequences such as altered metabolic activity, short-chain fatty acid production, resistance gene enrichment, or impaired colonization resistance.

rubrics.title: Time course and reversibility
rubrics.description: The answer must address whether microbiota perturbations are transient or persistent and summarize how quickly recovery occurs after treatment, including any evidence of long-term or incomplete recovery.

rubrics.title: Confounders and treatment context
rubrics.description: The answer must note key modifiers of the association, including dosage, treatment duration, combination therapy, baseline microbiota state, age, and other exposures that influence observed effects.

rubrics.title: Clinical and research relevance
rubrics.description: The answer must translate the evidence into practical implications for antibiotic choice, stewardship, and future research gaps, especially where certain classes may warrant greater microbiome caution.
